summary: Round 2 verify. Both round-1 minors are genuinely addressed: M4.36 no longer claims the drain net needs ten real seconds, it names the millisecond interrupted-join route, it says explicitly NOT to build the seam for the test, and it carries the 'nothing marks the closer entered join / slow, never wrong' caveat in the form I recorded it -- not flattened into a promise. I re-checked the two message defects against HEAD's code: the WARNING at BatchingSequencer.java:451-455 does precede a close gated on claimDelegateClose() at :473, and the InterruptedException catch at :444-446 leaves stopped==false, so both are real and injecting the timeout fixes neither. RE-RAN THIS ROUND at module scope (240 sequencer tests, 27 classes, failures=0 errors=0 both times): M4.36's deletion of failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) from close():459, and M4.37(a)'s replacement of terminalFailure()'s body with a causeless 'this sequencer is closed'. Both still survive. CARRIED FORWARD from round 1, where I ran it under a full ./gradlew test: M4.37(b), catch (Throwable) -> catch (Exception) in closeDelegateQuietly. Two minors, both prose, neither blocking. The substantive one is measured: M4.36's claim that the net is pinnable today is TRUE, but the mechanism it prescribes -- a latch -- is broken by close()'s own interrupt, and I measured a test built literally to that recipe letting the mutation through.

findings.title: M4.36's prescribed recipe, read literally, does NOT kill the mutation it is written for -- a latch pin is broken by close()'s own interrupt, and the committer's twin net then frees the caller
findings.detail: The row's conclusion is right and I measured it: the !stopped branch IS reachable in milliseconds today with no production change. The mechanism it names is not sufficient. close() calls committer.interrupt() at BatchingSequencer.java:424 BEFORE it joins, so a CountDownLatch.await() pin inside the delegate's commitAll -- 'pin the committer inside commitAll on a latch', which is my own round-1 wording adopted verbatim -- is broken by that very interrupt. The committer then leaves commitAll, exits the loop (running is already false), and its own finally net at :246 drains the queue itself, so the queued caller is freed whether or not close() still carries failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) at :459. MEASURED in my tree with a probe written to the recipe: with an interruptible CountDownLatch pin, 'queuedCallerFreedWithin4s=true' both unmutated AND with :459 deleted -- the mutation the row exists to pin SURVIVES the test the row prescribes. The same probe with the pin changed to Semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly(): freed unmutated, never freed with :459 deleted -- mutation killed, and reached in ~150 ms, not ten seconds. So the fix to the row is one clause: the pin must be insensitive to interrupts (acquireUninterruptibly, CompletableFuture.join, or a latch await retried through the flag), because close() interrupts the committer first. Minor, not blocking: the row is a todo, the claim it makes is true, and the implementer would find this the moment their red record refused to go red. Recording it so the next session does not spend the round rediscovering it.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks up M4.36, follows the row literally, pins the delegate's commitAll on a CountDownLatch, queues a second caller, interrupts the closing thread and asserts the caller is freed. The test passes. It also passes with failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) deleted from close():459 -- MEASURED, both variants run in my tree -- because close():424 interrupts the committer first, the latch await throws, and the committer's own finally net at :246 drains the queue instead. M4.36 is then marked done with the surviving mutation still surviving and a green test standing where the pin was supposed to be.

findings.title: The done row calls 203,911,796 ns 'the margin'; it is where the mutation LANDS, and the margin both reviewers measured is ~96-100 ms
findings.detail: 'the margin M4.37 disputes was measured at 203,911,796 ns against a 300 ms floor'. That number is mine, and it is the ELAPSED time of theRealClockTimerActuallyWaitsItsInterval under the 200 ms-constant mutation, not a margin. The margin against the 300 ms floor is 96,088,204 ns. My round-1 record says '203.9 ms against a 300 ms floor, ~96 ms of margin, not ~400'; the production reviewer measured the same quantity independently and wrote 'floor margin is 100 ms'. As written the row records a margin twice what either reviewer measured, and makes M4.37's disputed '~400 ms of slack' look 2x off when it is 4x off -- it understates the correction it is recording. M4.37's own row (backlog-notes.md:297), which is what an implementer reads, states it correctly as a landing point ('measured at 202ms against a 300ms floor'), so nothing downstream is misled. Secondary: nanosecond precision on a single wall-clock run implies a repeatability the two runs disprove -- 202 ms at M4.7 round 8, 203.9 ms here, same mutation. 'measured at ~204 ms against a 300 ms floor, leaving ~96 ms of margin rather than ~400' states exactly what was done. Everything else the row claims about round 1 checks out against both records: both reviewers did catch M4.36's root-cause claim AND its ten-second claim independently (R1 names both), M4.35's backwards clause was R2, the escaped quotes were T2, and 'BOTH REVIEWERS RE-RAN ALL THREE' is true of both records rather than an assumption.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone later asks how much slack theRealClockTimerActuallyWaitsItsInterval's 300 ms floor really has against the 200 ms-constant mutation, greps the done row, reads 204 ms of margin, and concludes the floor has twice the headroom two reviewers actually measured (~96 ms). Lowering the interval or moving the floor on that basis narrows a bound that already discriminates by less than 100 ms, and the mutation the floor exists to catch starts landing above it.
